questions.q: What does .cache() actually save you from?
options: It permanently saves the DataFrame to disk instead of memory
Recomputing the same lazy transformation plan from scratch every time a new action runs against that DataFrame
It prevents the DataFrame from ever being filtered again
It automatically removes duplicate rows
questions.explain: This directly follows from Lesson 34's lazy evaluation — every action normally re-runs the whole plan.

questions.q: What's the key difference between .repartition() and .coalesce()?
options: coalesce() can increase partition count, repartition() cannot
They are exactly identical in every situation
repartition() can increase or decrease partition count and always shuffles; coalesce() can only decrease, avoiding a full shuffle where possible
repartition() only works on DataFrames read from Parquet
questions.explain: coalesce() is the cheaper choice specifically for reducing partition count before a final write.

questions.q: What is a shuffle in Spark?
options: The process of converting a DataFrame to a Pandas DataFrame
Spark physically moving data between worker nodes so rows sharing a key end up on the same machine, required by joins and groupBy
A random reordering of rows with no real performance impact
A step that only happens when reading data, never during a join
questions.explain: This is real network and disk I/O across the cluster — usually the single most expensive part of a Spark job.

questions.q: How does wrapping the small side of a join in broadcast() help performance?
options: It has no real performance benefit and is purely stylistic
It sends a full copy of the small table to every worker, avoiding the need to shuffle the large table across the cluster at all
It converts the join into a union() instead
It deletes the small table entirely and estimates the join results
questions.explain: This works well specifically when one side, like Lesson 55's zones table, is small enough to fit comfortably in memory.

questions.q: According to the course recap, what does Chapter 4 (PySpark) build directly on top of?
options: Nothing from earlier chapters — PySpark syntax is entirely independent of Spark's architecture
A completely separate tool unrelated to anything else in this course
Chapter 3's Spark architecture concepts (partitions, lazy evaluation, transformations/actions) applied as real, hands-on method calls
Only Chapter 1's storage concepts, with no relation to Chapters 2 or 3
questions.explain: This is the course's central throughline: Chapter 3 explained the concepts, Chapter 4 is where they became real code.
